candidates.printedLatin: nunquam credendus est nullos de caetero scientiae profectus impertiri, ad innovandos sensus hominis interioris?
candidates.englishAsRendered: is he who unceasingly brings forth new fruits for the refreshment of the outward man never to be believed to impart no further advances of knowledge, for the renewing of the senses of the inward man?
candidates.conjecture: nunquam → nunquid (a double negative, nunquam + nullos, stacks to assert the opposite of the prologue's whole thesis that God still grants new understanding)
candidates.whyContradiction: The entire prologue argues FOR fresh understanding beyond the Fathers ('Non est ergo magnum, vel mirum si in uno aliquo aliquid possumus addere'); as printed, the rhetorical question doubly negates itself into a flat denial that any new advance is ever to be believed, contradicting the very case Richard is making in the sentences immediately before and after.

candidates.printedLatin: Nec arula per aditum dictorum ostiorum inferebatur, et super craticulae bases, et super ostium limen imponebatur
candidates.englishAsRendered: Nor was the hearth brought in through the approach of the said doors, and laid upon the bases of the grate and upon the threshold of the door
candidates.conjecture: Nec → Nam ("For the hearth WAS brought in...")
candidates.whyContradiction: Richard's whole surrounding argument is that the little doors (ostiola) exist precisely so the hearth can be brought in and laid on the grate's bases — he says so explicitly eight lines later at what corresponds to 0222D ('quod de ostiolorum aditu dictum est'). As printed, the sentence flatly denies the hearth was ever brought in through those doors, which guts the reason he gives for the doors' existence.

candidates.printedLatin: Superfluum vero videtur quod expressio materiae reperitur.
candidates.englishAsRendered: But it seems superfluous that a specification of the material is found.
candidates.conjecture: Non superfluum ("it does not seem superfluous")
candidates.whyContradiction: Richard immediately goes on to build an argument out of exactly this specification — the material named twice, olive wood at the oracle against fir at the temple entrance — treating it as significant, not superfluous; as printed he first dismisses as pointless the very detail he then argues from.
